title: President – rules
h1sub: card game: rules & how to play
sub: The hostel classic: get rid of your cards fast, climb to the top – and make the Scum hand over their best cards.

seo.rulesT: President card game rules – how to play
seo.rulesD: How to play President (Scum): dealing, singles and pairs, the ranks from President to Scum, the card swap and popular house rules.
seo.strategyT: President strategy guide – tips to reach the top
seo.strategyD: The President card game strategy guide: swap smart, control the lead, play pairs and 2s at the right moment and climb out of Scum.

goal: Goal: be the first to play all your cards. Whoever goes out first is President in the next round – whoever is left holding cards becomes the Scum.
setupLead: One normal deck of 52 cards, no jokers, and 4 to 7 players. Three players work too; from about 8 players, shuffle two decks together.
rankLead: Suits don't matter, only the rank counts. The 3 is the lowest card – and the 2 is the highest, even above the ace.
rankAlt: Card order from lowest to highest: 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, jack, queen, king, ace, 2
dealP: Shuffle and deal the whole deck clockwise, one card at a time. Some players may get one card more than others – that's fine. Everyone picks up and sorts their hand.
leadP: In the first round, whoever holds the 3 of clubs starts and includes it in their opening play (alone or with other 3s). From the second round on, the President starts. The starter leads: they put down one card or several cards of the same rank.
comboAlt: Possible leads: a single 5, a pair of 8s or three jacks
beatLead: Then it goes clockwise. On your turn you either beat what is on top or you pass.
s1p: A single card goes on a single card, a pair on a pair, three of a kind on three of a kind. Four of a kind can only be beaten by a higher four.
s2p: Your cards have to be higher than the ones on top. Equal is not enough: a pair of 7s does not beat a pair of 7s.
s3p: You may always pass, even if you could play. Passing doesn't lock you out: when your turn comes round again in the same trick, you may play again.
btTableAlt: On the table: a pair of 7s
btNo1: A single king: one card is not a pair
trickP: The trick is over when someone plays and everyone else passes in a row. The cards go face down to one side, and whoever played last leads the next trick with anything they like. If that player has just played their last card, the next player who still has cards leads.
endH: End of the round and ranks
endLead: Whoever plays their last card is out and watches the rest. The others play on until only one player still has cards. The order in which you go out decides your rank for the next round.
ladderNote: With four players there are no Citizens. With three players there is no Vice: just President, Citizen and Scum.
seatP: Many groups now change seats so everyone sits clockwise in order of rank: the President on the best chair, the Vice-President to their left, the Scum to their right. Too much moving around? Just stay where you are – the swap and the lead still work the same way.
swLead: From the second round on, your rank matters: before anyone plays, the bottom players have to give away their best cards.
swAlt: The Scum gives the President their two highest cards, a 2 and an ace. The President gives back two cards of their choice, a 4 and a 6.
w1p: The Scum collects, shuffles and deals – the least popular job at the table.
w2h: Scum and President swap two cards
w2p: The Scum gives the President their two highest cards. The President gives back any two cards they don't want.
w3h: Vice-Scum and Vice-President swap one card
w3p: The same with one card: the Vice-Scum hands over their highest card and gets one card of the Vice-President's choice back. Citizens keep their hands.
w4p: Then the President starts the first trick with anything they like.
swWhy: That's why it is so hard to get away from the bottom: the Scum loses their 2s and aces and gets weak cards in return. But with clever play you can still climb up – and that's what makes the game fun.
varLead: Almost every hostel plays President a little differently. Agree before the first deal which of these rules you use. Without them, you play the basic game described above.
var1: Revolution: whoever plays four of a kind turns the card order upside down for the rest of the round – the 3 becomes the highest card and the 2 the lowest. The next four of a kind turns it back.
var2: Equal skips: you may also play cards of the same rank as the ones on top. The next player is then skipped.
var3: A 2 clears the table: a single 2 beats anything, even pairs or three of a kind. The trick ends at once and whoever played the 2 leads again.
var4: Passing is final: whoever passes sits out until the trick is over.
var5: No going out on a 2: whoever plays a 2 as their last card automatically becomes the Scum.
var6: Jokers: two jokers in the deck rank above the 2. Some groups use them as wild cards instead.
var7: The Scum leads: instead of the President, the Scum starts the first trick – a small consolation after the swap.
faq1q: Do I have to play if I can?
faq1a: No. Passing is always allowed, even with a good card in your hand. Keeping a pair of aces for later is often the better move.
faq2q: Can I break up a pair?
faq2a: Yes. If someone plays a single card, you may play one card from your pair. You just don't have the pair any more.
faq3a: In the basic game the 2 is simply the highest rank: a single 2 beats any single card, but a pair of aces is only beaten by a pair of 2s. With the house rule “A 2 clears the table”, a single 2 is enough.
faq4q: What happens when I play my last card?
faq4a: You're out and get your rank for the next round. If nobody beats your last cards, the next player who still has cards leads the new trick.
faq5q: How does it work with three players?
faq5a: There is a President, a Citizen and a Scum. Only the President and the Scum swap, two cards as usual.
faq6q: Who deals in the first round?
faq6a: Anyone. From the second round on, the Scum always deals.
faq7a: Whenever you like – you just keep playing new rounds. If you want a winner: 2 points for the President, 1 for the Vice-President, and the first to reach 11 points wins.
faq8q: Is President the same as Asshole?
faq8a: More or less: they belong to the same family of games, and many groups use the names for the same thing. The ranks and house rules just have different names from place to place.

strategy.sub: The President strategy guide. The rules take two minutes to learn, but knowing when to pass, what to swap and how to keep the lead makes all the difference.
strategy.principle: President is a game of control. High cards don’t just beat a trick – they buy you the lead, and the lead is how you get rid of weak cards. Count what’s left, save your top cards for the moments that matter and never let low single cards trap you at the end.
strategy.swapH: Before the round: the card swap
strategy.swapLead: The Scum has no choice and must hand over their two highest cards. As President or Vice-President, however, choosing what to give back is your biggest decision before a single card hits the table.
strategy.giveH: What to give back to the Scum:
give: Unpaired low cards first (3, 4, 5, 6). Single low cards are the hardest to shed later because you need the lead to play them. Handing back a lone 5 and 7 cleans up your hand right away.
Keep your pairs intact. Never break a pair of 4s just to give away a lower card. A low pair disappears in a single lead – two mismatched single cards cost you two separate turns.
Give two different ranks. Avoid handing back two cards of the same value. Giving the Scum a pair of 4s hands them a free combo they can dump in one move.
Check your new sets first. Look at the cards the Scum gave you before choosing. If their ace pairs up with your own ace, protect that pair and trim loose low singletons instead.
As Vice-President (one card): The same logic applies – return your lowest unpaired card, not half of a pair.
strategy.notGive: What not to give back: a matching pair (like two 4s) or a high card that breaks up a strong set. Giving the Scum ready-made pairs saves them turns – and leaving yourself with awkward singletons hurts more than holding a low pair.
strategy.exAlt: Example swap. President's hand: a pair of 4s, a single 5, a single 7, an ace and a 2. After the swap: you keep the pair of 4s, the ace and the 2, and give the unpaired 5 and 7 to the Scum.
strategy.exWhy: Why? Instead of breaking the pair of 4s – or handing both 4s to the Scum as a ready-made pair – you return the two unmatched single cards (5 and 7). Your pair of 4s goes out in one move, while the Scum is stuck with two loose low cards.
strategy.exVariant: 1-card swap (Vice-President): With only one card to give back, pick the lone 5 and keep the pair of 4s together.
strategy.exVariantAlt: 1-card swap: keep the pair of 4s and return the single 5

items: Read your hand shape first. Before playing a card, check whether your hand leans toward pairs and triples or single cards. Try to steer tricks into the format that empties your hand fastest.
Lead low, not high. When you win the lead early, open with your lowest single card or lowest pair. If someone beats it, great – you just shed dead weight without spending a high card.

Pass freely – passing costs nothing. You are never locked out of a trick by passing (unless you play the “passing is final” house rule). Let others burn their kings and aces early while you wait for a cheaper opening.
Keep pairs and triples together. Splitting a pair of 9s just to beat a single 7 weakens your hand. Sets clear two or three cards at once and are much harder for opponents to beat.

Playing from the bottom (as Scum): Don’t fight the President head-on in the first tricks. Pass on high leads, slip your medium cards out whenever the table stays low, and wait for the top players to exhaust each other’s 2s and aces.
Count the 2s and aces. There are only four 2s and four aces in the deck. Once all four 2s are gone, an ace guarantees you the lead; once the aces are out too, a king becomes unbeatable.
Track high pairs. Remember which high pairs (queens, kings, aces, 2s) have already been played. Halfway through a round, even a pair of jacks or queens often wins the trick outright.
Break the leader’s rhythm. If one player keeps leading pairs and winning them back, spend a strong pair once to steal the lead – then switch to singles or triples to throw off their hand.

Save your 2 for a real payoff. Don’t drop a 2 just to beat a single 6 if you have nothing weak left to lead next. A 2 is most valuable when winning the lead lets you clear low cards or shift the format.
Watch who is running low. Keep an eye on hand sizes. If the player to your left is down to two or three cards, think twice before leading singles or pairs that match what they’ve been winning with.

Plan your final two turns together. Before taking the lead with a 2 or an ace, check how you’ll go out. The cleanest finish: steal the lead with your top card, then immediately drop your final pair or low card to end your round.

Finish on your weakest card, not your strongest. Holding a 2 and a lone 4? Win the lead with the 2 and go out on the 4 – nobody can stop your last lead. Getting stuck with the 4 at the end is only dangerous if you lose the lead first.
Keep a pair for the finish. Closing the round with a pair (like two 6s) after winning a trick clears two cards in one move and avoids getting trapped with a lone low card.

Fight for every rank. Even if another player is guaranteed to finish first, stay sharp. Finishing second (Vice-President) earns you a top card in the next swap instead of losing one – and staying out of Scum is always worth a careful endgame.
Remember your house rules. If your table plays with “no going out on a 2”, make sure your 2 wins the second-to-last trick and is never your final card.

strategy.cardsLead: President has no special powers in the basic rules, yet certain ranks and sets decide almost every round. Knowing when to hold them – and when to spend them – separates the President from the Scum.

cards.p: The highest card in the deck. On singles, a 2 cannot be beaten and guarantees you the next lead.
items: Save it to take control right when you need to dump low singletons or close out the round.
Holding two 2s? A pair of 2s beats any pair – don’t split them unless a single 2 wins you the round.
With the house rule “A 2 clears the table”, a single 2 beats pairs and triples too, making it even more precious.

cards.p: Second-highest rank, and unbeatable as soon as the 2s are gone. Use single aces to draw out opponents’ 2s, or keep a pair of aces to lock down pair tricks.
A pair clears two cards in a single turn. Even low pairs (like two 4s) are far easier to shed than loose singletons, while high pairs (queens, kings, aces) frequently win the trick outright.

cards.h: Three of a kind – Trick killers
cards.p: Triples are very hard to beat – even three 5s often clear the table and hand the lead right back to you. Avoid breaking a triple into a pair plus a single card unless you have no other play.
The 3 of clubs starts the first round – a great excuse to drop all your 3s together right away. Use every early lead to push out single 3s, 4s and 5s before the endgame begins.

Clears four cards in one shot and can only be beaten by a higher four. Playing with the Revolution house rule? Four of a kind flips the card order so 3s become the best cards – hold it if you have low cards ready to take over.

mistakes: Giving the Scum a pair in the swap. Returning two 4s instead of a 4 and a 6 hands the Scum a free combo. Always give back mismatched single cards when you can.
Breaking pairs for small tricks. Splitting a pair of 10s just to beat a single 8 leaves you with an awkward single card and gives up a pair that could have won a trick later.
Wasting 2s and aces early. Spending your 2 on the first trick just to win a lead you don’t need leaves you helpless when the endgame decides the ranks.
Never passing. Just because you can beat a card doesn’t mean you should. Passing is free and lets the others burn their high cards on each other.
Not counting 2s and aces. If you don’t notice all four 2s have been played, you’ll hold back your ace too long instead of taking the lead at the right moment.

Getting stuck with a low singleton at the end. Playing your high cards first and leaving a lone 3 or 4 as your last card forces you to pass until everyone else goes out – always clear weak cards while you still have a high card to win the lead.
